title: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE)
usedFor:
• Screening for cognitive impairment and dementia.
  • Tracking cognitive changes over time.
howTo:
• Position: Patient sitting in a quiet room.
  • Action: Administer questions testing orientation, registration, attention, calculation, recall, and language (max score 30).
extra: Highly dependent on educational level and age.
references: • Folstein, M. F., et al. (1975). Mini-Mental State Exam.

title: Visual Acuity Test (Snellen Chart)
usedFor: • Assessing visual acuity (central vision) controlled by Cranial Nerve II.
howTo:
• Position: Patient stands 20 feet (6 meters) from the Snellen chart.
  • Action: Have the patient cover one eye and read the smallest line of letters they can see. Repeat with other eye.
result:
• Normal: 20/20 vision (or equivalent).
  • Abnormal: Inability to read standard lines, indicating optic pathway pathology or refractive error.
references: • Snellen, H. (1862). Test-types for the determination of the acuteness of vision.

title: Pronator Drift Test
usedFor: • Detecting subtle upper motor neuron (pyramidal tract) weakness.
howTo:
• Position: Patient stands or sits with eyes closed.
  • Action: Have patient extend both arms straight forward with palms up for 20-30 seconds.
result: • Positive Result (Abnormal): One arm drifts downward and pronates (palms turn inward/downward), indicating contralateral corticospinal tract lesion.

title: Patellar Reflex Test (Knee Jerk)
usedFor: • Assessing the integrity of the L2, L3, and L4 spinal nerve segments.
howTo:
• Position: Patient sits with legs dangling freely over the edge of the examination table.
  • Action: Tap the patellar tendon directly below the patella using a reflex hammer.
result:
• Normal: Extension of the knee (graded as 2+).
  • Hyporeflexia (0 or 1+): Lower motor neuron lesion.
  • Hyperreflexia (3+ or 4+): Upper motor neuron lesion.
extra: Jendrassik maneuver can be used to reinforce the reflex if it is difficult to elicit.

title: Light Touch Examination
usedFor: • Assessing the spinothalamic tract and dorsal columns.
howTo:
• Position: Patient sitting or supine with eyes closed.
  • Action: Touch the patient's skin lightly using a wisp of cotton wool at various dermatomal levels.
result:
• Normal: Patient perceives touch symmetrically in all areas.
  • Abnormal: Anesthesia or hypoesthesia in specific distributions.
references: • Campbell, W. W. (2012). DeJong's The Neurologic Examination.

title: Finger-to-Nose Test
usedFor: • Assessing cerebellar coordination and detecting dysmetria/intention tremor.
howTo:
• Position: Patient sitting facing the examiner.
  • Action: Have the patient touch their nose with their index finger, then touch the examiner's finger (which moves positions), repeatedly.
result:
• Normal: Smooth, accurate movements.
  • Abnormal (Dysmetria): Overshooting or undershooting the target, accompanied by intention tremor, suggesting cerebellar pathology.

title: Romberg Test
usedFor: • Differentiating sensory ataxia (proprioceptive loss) from cerebellar ataxia.
howTo:
• Position: Patient stands with feet together and arms at sides.
  • Action: Observe balance first with eyes open, then have patient close eyes for 30 seconds.
result: • Positive Romberg (Abnormal): Patient stands steadily with eyes open but loses balance/sways significantly with eyes closed, indicating sensory ataxia (dorsal column pathology).
extra: Ensure you stand close to the patient to catch them in case they fall.
references: • Romberg, M. H. (1846). Lehrbuch der Nervenkrankheiten des Menschen.

title: Tandem Gait Test
usedFor: • Detecting subtle balance and gait abnormalities, especially midline cerebellar dysfunction.
howTo: • Action: Have the patient walk in a straight line placing the heel of one foot directly in front of the toe of the other (heel-to-toe walking).
result:
• Normal: Smooth walking without loss of balance.
  • Abnormal: Inability to walk straight, frequent stepping out of line, indicating cerebellar ataxia or vestibular dysfunction.

title: Phalen's Test
usedFor: • Screening for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (median nerve compression).
howTo: • Action: Have the patient hold both wrists in maximum forced flexion (pressing the dorsal surfaces of their hands together) for 60 seconds.
result: • Positive Result (Abnormal): Tingling or numbness in the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger.

title: Shoulder Abduction (C5 Testing)
usedFor: • Evaluating the C5 spinal nerve root (Deltoid muscle).
howTo:
• Position: Patient sits with arms abducted to 90 degrees.
  • Action: Apply downward resistance on the upper arms while instructing the patient to resist.
result:
• Normal: Strong contraction (Grade 5/5).
  • Abnormal: Weakness in abduction, suggesting C5 radiculopathy or axillary nerve lesion.

title: Thumb Sensation Assessment (C6)
usedFor: • Evaluating sensory integrity of the C6 nerve root.
howTo: • Action: Assess light touch and pinprick sensation on the dorsal surface of the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
result: • Normal: Intact, symmetrical sensation compared to the opposite thumb and reference dermatomes.

title: Kernig's Sign Test
usedFor: • Evaluating for meningeal irritation (e.g., meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage).
howTo:
• Position: Patient supine.
  • Action: Flex the patient's hip and knee to 90 degrees, then slowly extend the knee.
result: • Positive Result (Abnormal): Resistance and pain in the hamstrings, limiting extension of the knee, indicating meningeal irritation.
references: • Kernig, W. (1882). Ueber eine neue Methode zur Untersuchung von Meningitiskranken.

title: Orthostatic Blood Pressure Measurement
usedFor: • Evaluating autonomic stability and detecting orthostatic hypotension.
howTo: • Action: Measure blood pressure and heart rate after the patient has been supine for 5 minutes, then repeat after they stand for 1 and 3 minutes.
result: • Abnormal: Drop in systolic BP >= 20 mmHg or diastolic BP >= 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing, indicating autonomic failure.

title: Ideomotor Apraxia Examination
usedFor: • Evaluating higher-order motor planning deficits (dominant parietal lobe).
howTo: • Action: Instruct the patient to perform pantomime gestures on command (e.g., "Show me how you would blow out a match" or "comb your hair").
result: • Abnormal: Inability to carry out the motor command despite having normal raw motor strength, comprehension, and coordination, indicating apraxia.

title: National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS)
usedFor: • Standardizing and quantifying the severity of acute ischemic stroke.
howTo: • Action: Grade 11 items covering level of consciousness, gaze, vision, motor drift, ataxia, sensory, language, dysarthria, and inattention (scores range from 0 to 42).
references: • Brott, T., et al. (1989). Measurements of acute cerebral infarction.
